<style>

  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}

    font-size:17px;line-height:1.65}

  code{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;
    background:#0b0f16;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:4px;color:#f0c987;font-size:0.92em}

  h2{font-size:1.6rem;margin:3.2rem 0 0.8rem;color:#fff;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding-bottom:.4rem}
  h3{font-size:1.15rem;margin:1.8rem 0 .6rem;color:var(--yellow)}
  p{margin:0.7rem 0}
  .sub{color:var(--mute);margin-top:0;margin-bottom:2rem}
  .widget{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:10px;
    padding:1rem 1.1rem 1.2rem;margin:1.2rem 0}
  .widget .hd{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:baseline;margin-bottom:.6rem;gap:.8rem;flex-wrap:wrap}
  .widget .hd .ttl{font-weight:600;color:#fff;font-size:.95rem;letter-spacing:.02em;text-transform:uppercase}
  .widget .hd .hint{color:var(--mute);font-size:.85rem}
  .row{display:flex;gap:.6rem;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:center;margin:.4rem 0}
  .row label{color:var(--mute);font-size:.88rem}
  input[type="text"],input[type="number"],select{
    background:#0b0f16;color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:6px;padding:.35rem .55rem;font-family:inherit;font-size:.95rem}
  input[type="range"]{accent-color:var(--yellow);flex:1;max-width:260px}
  button{background:var(--panel2);color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:6px;padding:.35rem .7rem;cursor:pointer;font:inherit}
  button:hover{background:#242c3e}
  button.active{background:var(--yellow);color:#111;border-color:var(--yellow)}

    padding:.6rem .8rem;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:.92rem;color:#cbd5e1;
    min-height:1.6em;white-space:pre-wrap;word-break:break-word}
  .pill{display:inline-block;background:var(--panel2);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:999px;padding:1px 8px;font-size:.82rem;color:var(--mute);margin-right:4px}
  .note{border-left:3px solid var(--violet);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#d8d2ef;background:#1a1828;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  .ok{border-left:3px solid var(--green);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#d5ebc8;background:#1a2418;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  .bad{border-left:3px solid var(--pink);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#f4d2c7;background:#2a1a18;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  svg{display:block;margin:0 auto;max-width:100%}
  svg text{fill:var(--ink);font-family:inherit}
  nav.toc{position:sticky;top:0;background:rgba(15,18,24,.93);backdrop-filter:blur(8px);
    border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding:.6rem 1rem;z-index:10;
    display:flex;gap:1rem;flex-wrap:wrap;font-size:.9rem}
  nav.toc a{color:var(--mute);text-decoration:none}
  nav.toc a:hover{color:var(--yellow)}

  aside.sidetoc{position:fixed;top:4.2rem;
    left:max(1rem, calc(50% - 440px - 220px));
    width:200px;max-height:calc(100vh - 6rem);overflow-y:auto;
    padding-right:1rem;border-right:1px solid var(--line);
    font-size:.88rem;z-index:5}
  aside.sidetoc .sidetoc-title{font-size:.7rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute);margin:0 0 .5rem;padding-bottom:.35rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line)}
  aside.sidetoc ol{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:0}
  aside.sidetoc li{margin:0}
  aside.sidetoc a{display:block;padding:.3rem .5rem;color:var(--mute);text-decoration:none;
    border-left:2px solid transparent;line-height:1.35;
    transition:color 120ms ease, border-color 120ms ease}
  aside.sidetoc a:hover{color:var(--ink)}
  aside.sidetoc a.active{color:var(--yellow);border-left-color:var(--yellow)}
  @media (max-width:1180px){ aside.sidetoc{display:none} }
  @media (min-width:1181px){ nav.toc a[href^="#"]{display:none} }

  .small{font-size:.88rem;color:var(--mute)}
  footer{color:var(--mute);font-size:.88rem;text-align:center;margin-top:4rem}

  table.plain th{color:var(--mute);font-weight:500}

  aside.callback{
    margin:1.2rem 0;padding:.7rem 1rem;
    background:rgba(88,196,221,0.05);
    border-left:3px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--cyan) 45%, transparent);
    border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;
    font-size:.93rem;
  }
  aside.callback .ttl{
    font-size:.68rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);margin-bottom:.3rem;font-weight:600;
  }
  aside.callback ul{margin:0;padding-left:1.1rem}
  aside.callback ul li{margin:.15rem 0}
  aside.callback a{color:inherit}
/* callback-css-auto-end */
  details.changelog{
    margin:2rem 0 1rem;padding:.6rem .9rem;
    background:rgba(0,0,0,0.22);
    border-radius:6px;
    font-size:.85rem;
  }
  details.changelog summary{
    cursor:pointer;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;
    font-size:.7rem;color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);
  }
  details.changelog table{margin-top:.5rem;border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;font-size:.82rem}
  details.changelog td{padding:.2rem .6rem;border-bottom:1px dashed rgba(255,255,255,0.07);vertical-align:top}
  details.changelog td:first-child{color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);white-space:nowrap;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
  aside.related{
    margin:1.2rem 0;padding:.7rem 1rem;
    background:color-mix(in srgb, var(--mute) 6%, transparent);
    border-left:3px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--mute) 55%, transparent);
    border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;
    font-size:.93rem;
  }
  aside.related .ttl{
    font-size:.68rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);margin-bottom:.3rem;font-weight:600;
  }
  aside.related > div{margin:.15rem 0}
  aside.related .more{color:var(--mute);font-style:italic}
  aside.related a{color:inherit}
  /* display-prefs-css-auto-begin */
  html[data-hide-widgets] .widget { display: none !important; }
  html[data-hide-quizzes] .quiz { display: none !important; }
  html[data-hide-lineage] .lineage-strip { display: none !important; }

  .mv-display-toggle--off { opacity: 0.35; }
  /* display-prefs-css-auto-end */

From Itô's lemma to Black–Scholes to Merton's portfolio problem: how the SDE skeleton built in stochastic calculus prices contingent claims by no-arbitrage replication, and how dynamic-programming over a controlled diffusion solves the optimal-investment problem via the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation.

1. The Black–Scholes model

The 1973 model of Black, Scholes, and Merton was the first arbitrage-free pricing theory rigorous enough to be calibrated against quoted market prices. It rests on three structural choices: (i) the asset $S_t$ follows geometric Brownian motion with constant drift $\mu$ and volatility $\sigma$, (ii) trading is frictionless and continuous in time, (iii) there is a riskless bond earning rate $r$.

The driving SDE is $$dS_t \;=\; \mu\,S_t\,dt + \sigma\,S_t\,dB_t, \qquad S_0=s.$$ Applying Itô to $\log S_t$ (see §Itô's formula) gives the closed form $$S_t = s\exp\!\bigl((\mu-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)t+\sigma B_t\bigr),$$ so $\log S_t$ is Gaussian, $S_t$ stays positive almost surely, and the mean grows like $s e^{\mu t}$ while the median grows like $s e^{(\mu-\sigma^2/2)t}$ — the lognormal mean–median gap is the "volatility drag."

No-arbitrage pricing of a European call. A European call on $S$ with strike $K$ and maturity $T$ pays $(S_T-K)^+$. The Black–Scholes formula prices it at time $t<T$ as $$C(S,t) \;=\; S\,\Phi(d_1) \;-\; Ke^{-r(T-t)}\Phi(d_2),$$ with $$d_1 \;=\; \frac{\log(S/K)+(r+\sigma^2/2)(T-t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T-t}}, \qquad d_2 \;=\; d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T-t},$$ and $\Phi$ the standard-normal CDF. The formula does not depend on $\mu$ — the empirically untestable real-world drift drops out, because the price equals the cost of a self-financing hedging portfolio, which only uses $r$ and $\sigma$.

The thumb rule. For at-the-money ($S=K$) and zero rate, $d_1=\sigma\sqrt{T}/2$, $d_2=-d_1$, so $C\approx S\cdot 2\Phi'(0)\cdot d_1 \approx 0.4\,S\,\sigma\sqrt{T}$. A 1-year ATM option on a 20%-vol stock is worth roughly 8% of the underlying — useful for sanity-checking quotes in your head.

/* §1 — Geometric Brownian motion ensemble */
(function(){
  const svg=$('#gbm-svg'), out=$('#gbm-out');
  const muIn=$('#gbm-mu'), sigIn=$('#gbm-sig'), KIn=$('#gbm-K');
  const muV=$('#gbm-muv'), sigV=$('#gbm-sigv'), KV=$('#gbm-Kv');
  const W=760, H=320, x0=60, x1=W-30, y0=30, y1=H-40;
  const T=2.0, N=400, s0=1.0;
  let seeds=null;
  function genSeeds(K){
    const arr=[];
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++){
      const z=new Float64Array(N);
      for(let i=0;i<N;i++) z[i]=randn();
      arr.push(z);
    }
    return arr;
  }
  function path(z, mu, sig){
    const dt=T/N; const Xp=new Float64Array(N+1); Xp[0]=s0;
    for(let i=1;i<=N;i++){
      Xp[i] = Xp[i-1]*Math.exp((mu-0.5*sig*sig)*dt + sig*Math.sqrt(dt)*z[i-1]);
    }
    return Xp;
  }
  function draw(){
    const mu=+muIn.value, sig=+sigIn.value, K=+KIn.value;
    muV.textContent='μ = '+mu.toFixed(2);
    sigV.textContent='σ = '+sig.toFixed(2);
    KV.textContent='K = '+K;
    if(!seeds || seeds.length<K) seeds=genSeeds(Math.max(K,40));
    const paths=[];
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++) paths.push(path(seeds[k], mu, sig));
    svg.innerHTML='';
    let mn=Infinity, mx=-Infinity;
    for(const p of paths) for(const v of p){ if(v<mn)mn=v; if(v>mx)mx=v; }
    mn=Math.max(0, mn-0.08*(mx-mn));
    mx=mx+0.10*(mx-mn);
    const X=i=>x0 + (i/N)*(x1-x0);
    const Y=v=>y1 - (v-mn)/(mx-mn)*(y1-y0);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x0,y1:y1,x2:x1,y2:y1,stroke:'var(--line)'}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x0,y1:y0,x2:x0,y2:y1,stroke:'var(--line)'}));
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++){
      let d='';
      for(let i=0;i<=N;i++){ d += (i===0?'M':'L')+X(i)+','+Y(paths[k][i])+' '; }
      svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d,fill:'none',stroke:'var(--violet)','stroke-width':0.7,'stroke-opacity':0.5}));
    }
    let dm='';
    for(let i=0;i<=N;i++){ const t=i/N*T; dm+=(i===0?'M':'L')+X(i)+','+Y(s0*Math.exp(mu*t))+' '; }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:dm,fill:'none',stroke:'var(--pink)','stroke-width':2}));
    let dmd='';
    for(let i=0;i<=N;i++){ const t=i/N*T; dmd+=(i===0?'M':'L')+X(i)+','+Y(s0*Math.exp((mu-0.5*sig*sig)*t))+' '; }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:dmd,fill:'none',stroke:'var(--cyan)','stroke-width':2,'stroke-dasharray':'4 3'}));
    const lg=SVG('g',{transform:'translate(80,40)'});
    function le(yy,col,dash,lab){
      const ln=SVG('line',{x1:0,y1:yy,x2:18,y2:yy,stroke:col,'stroke-width':2});
      if(dash) ln.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray',dash);
      lg.appendChild(ln);
      const t=SVG('text',{x:24,y:yy+4,'font-size':12,fill:col}); t.textContent=lab; lg.appendChild(t);
    }
    le(0,'var(--violet)',null,'sample paths');
    le(16,'var(--pink)',null,'mean  𝔼[Sₜ] = S₀ exp(μt)');
    le(32,'var(--cyan)','4 3','median');
    svg.appendChild(lg);
    for(let k=0;k<=4;k++){
      const xp=X(k*N/4);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xp,y1:y1,x2:xp,y2:y1+4,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:xp,y:y1+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=(k/4*T).toFixed(1); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    let s=0, ss=0;
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++){ const v=paths[k][N]; s+=v; ss+=v*v; }
    const m=s/K, va=ss/K - m*m;
    const meanTh=s0*Math.exp(mu*T);
    const medTh=s0*Math.exp((mu-0.5*sig*sig)*T);
    out.textContent =
      `dSₜ = μ Sₜ dt + σ Sₜ dBₜ,  S₀ = ${s0},  T = ${T}\n`+
      `closed form:  Sₜ = S₀ exp((μ−σ²/2) t + σ Bₜ)\n\n`+
      `at t = T:   theory mean = ${meanTh.toFixed(3)},  theory median = ${medTh.toFixed(3)}\n`+
      `              volatility drag (mean − median) = ${(meanTh-medTh).toFixed(3)}\n`+
      `   empirical mean (K=${K}) = ${m.toFixed(3)},  empirical var = ${va.toFixed(3)}`;
  }
  muIn.addEventListener('input', draw);
  sigIn.addEventListener('input', draw);
  KIn.addEventListener('input', draw);
  $('#gbm-new').addEventListener('click',()=>{seeds=null; draw();});
  draw();

2. The Black–Scholes PDE

Where does the formula come from? Two parallel derivations meet at the same equation. The first is delta-hedging. Hold one call $V(S,t)$ and short $\Delta_t=\partial_S V$ shares; the portfolio value $\Pi_t = V_t - \Delta_t S_t$ has differential (Itô): $$d\Pi_t \;=\; \Bigl(\partial_t V + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2\,\partial_{SS}V\Bigr)dt + \bigl(\partial_S V - \Delta_t\bigr)dS_t.$$ Choosing $\Delta_t=\partial_S V$ kills the stochastic term. The remaining $d\Pi_t$ is deterministic, so by no-arbitrage it must grow at the risk-free rate: $d\Pi_t = r\Pi_t\,dt$. Equating coefficients, $$\boxed{\;\partial_t V + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2\,\partial_{SS}V + rS\,\partial_S V - rV \;=\; 0\;}$$ with terminal condition $V(T,S)=(S-K)^+$ for a call. The second derivation is via Feynman–Kac applied to the risk-neutral SDE $dS_t=rS_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,d\tilde B_t$: the same PDE pops out as the generator equation for $V(t,S)=e^{-r(T-t)}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[g(S_T)\mid S_t=S]$. The two pictures — hedging and expectation under the right measure — are different aspects of the same operator.

Reduction to the heat equation. Substituting $S=Ke^x$, $\tau = \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2(T-t)$, $V=Ke^{-r(T-t)}e^{\alpha x+\beta\tau}u(x,\tau)$ for appropriate $\alpha,\beta$ collapses the PDE to $\partial_\tau u = \partial_{xx}u$. Black–Scholes is therefore the heat equation in disguise — and the closed form is the Gaussian convolution of the payoff.

  const W=760, H=320, xL=60, xR=W-30, yT=30, yB=H-40;
  function bsCall(S,K,r,sig,tau){
    if(tau<=1e-9) return Math.max(S-K,0);
    const sst=sig*Math.sqrt(tau);
    const d1=(Math.log(S/K)+(r+sig*sig/2)*tau)/sst;
    const d2=d1-sst;
    return S*normCdf(d1)-K*Math.exp(-r*tau)*normCdf(d2);
  }

    const K=+KIn.value, sig=+sigIn.value, r=+rIn.value, tau=+tauIn.value;

    sigV.textContent='σ = '+sig.toFixed(2);

    const Smin=Math.max(1, K*0.4), Smax=K*1.8;
    const X=s=>xL + (s-Smin)/(Smax-Smin)*(xR-xL);
    let Cmax=0;
    for(let i=0;i<=200;i++){
      const s=Smin+(i/200)*(Smax-Smin);
      const c=bsCall(s,K,r,sig,tau);
      if(c>Cmax) Cmax=c;

    const Y=c=>yB - (c/Cax)*(yB-yT);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:yB,x2:xR,y2:yB,stroke:'var(--line)'}));

    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:X(K),y1:yT,x2:X(K),y2:yB,stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-dasharray':'3 4','stroke-width':1}));
    const tk=SVG('text',{x:X(K),y:yT-6,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--yellow)'});
    tk.textContent='K='+K; svg.appendChild(tk);
    // payoff curve

      const s=Smin+(i/200)*(Smax-Smin);

      dp += (i===0?'M':'L')+X(s)+','+Y(c)+' ';

    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:dp,fill:'none',stroke:'var(--cyan)','stroke-width':1.3,'stroke-dasharray':'4 3'}));
    // BS price curve

    for(let i=0;i<=200;i++){
      const s=Smin+(i/200)*(Smax-Smin);
      const c=bsCall(s,K,r,sig,tau);
      db += (i===0?'M':'L')+X(s)+','+Y(c)+' ';
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:db,fill:'none',stroke:'var(--pink)','stroke-width':2}));
    // x-axis ticks: S
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const s=Smin+(i/4)*(Smax-Smin);
      const xp=X(s);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xp,y1:yB,x2:xp,y2:yB+4,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:xp,y:yB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});

3. Risk-neutral pricing and martingale measures

Girsanov's theorem provides a more conceptual restatement: drifts are a feature of the measure, not of the process. Under the historical measure $\mathbb{P}$ the asset has the real-world drift $\mu$, but a change of measure $$\frac{d\mathbb{Q}}{d\mathbb{P}} \;=\; \exp\!\Bigl(-\theta B_T - \tfrac{1}{2}\theta^2 T\Bigr), \qquad \theta \;=\; \frac{\mu-r}{\sigma}\quad\text{(market price of risk)}$$ turns $\tilde B_t = B_t + \theta t$ into a $\mathbb{Q}$-Brownian motion. Under $\mathbb{Q}$, $$dS_t \;=\; r S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,d\tilde B_t,$$ so the discounted price $\tilde S_t = e^{-rt}S_t$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-martingale. Risk-neutral pricing: $$V_0 \;=\; e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}\bigl[g(S_T)\bigr]$$ for any (suitably integrable) payoff $g$. The discount accounts for time-value; the change of measure encodes no-arbitrage.

This is the operating principle behind almost every modern derivatives desk: build a model in which the discounted underlying is a $\mathbb{Q}$-martingale, then price the derivative as a (discounted) $\mathbb{Q}$-expectation, computed by Monte Carlo or by solving the corresponding PDE.

Fundamental theorems of asset pricing. FTAP I: no arbitrage $\iff$ there exists an equivalent martingale measure (EMM) under which discounted prices are martingales. FTAP II: the market is complete (every payoff is replicable) $\iff$ the EMM is unique. In Black–Scholes, $\mathbb{Q}$ is unique and the market is complete. As soon as we add a second source of randomness — stochastic volatility, jumps, multi-factor rates — uniqueness fails and pricing acquires a degree of freedom that must be fixed by calibration.

<script>
/* §3 — Monte Carlo European call pricer */
(function(){
  const svg=$('#mc-svg'), out=$('#mc-out');
  const SIn=$('#mc-S'), KIn=$('#mc-K'), rIn=$('#mc-r'), sigIn=$('#mc-sig'), TIn=$('#mc-T'), NIn=$('#mc-N');
  const NV=$('#mc-Nv');
  const W=760, H=280, xL=60, xR=W-30, yT=30, yB=H-40;
  function normCdfLocal(x){
    const a1=0.254829592, a2=-0.284496736, a3=1.421413741, a4=-1.453152027, a5=1.061405429, p=0.3275911;
    const sign=x<0?-1:1; x=Math.abs(x)/Math.SQRT2;
    const t=1/(1+p*x);
    const y=1-(((((a5*t+a4)*t)+a3)*t+a2)*t+a1)*t*Math.exp(-x*x);
    return 0.5*(1+sign*y);
  }
  function bsCall(S,K,r,sig,T){
    if(T<=1e-9) return Math.max(S-K,0);
    const sst=sig*Math.sqrt(T);
    const d1=(Math.log(S/K)+(r+sig*sig/2)*T)/sst;
    const d2=d1-sst;
    return S*normCdfLocal(d1)-K*Math.exp(-r*T)*normCdfLocal(d2);
  }
  function run(){
    const S0=+SIn.value, K=+KIn.value, r=+rIn.value, sig=+sigIn.value, T=+TIn.value, N=+NIn.value;
    NV.textContent='N = '+N;
    const drift=(r-0.5*sig*sig)*T, vol=sig*Math.sqrt(T);
    const ST=new Float64Array(N);
    let pay=0, paysq=0;
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){
      const z=randn();
      const s=S0*Math.exp(drift+vol*z);
      ST[i]=s;
      const p=Math.max(s-K,0);
      pay+=p; paysq+=p*p;
    }
    const meanPay=pay/N;
    const mc=Math.exp(-r*T)*meanPay;
    const varPay=paysq/N - meanPay*meanPay;
    const se=Math.exp(-r*T)*Math.sqrt(varPay/N);
    const bs=bsCall(S0,K,r,sig,T);
    // histogram
    svg.innerHTML='';
    let mn=Infinity, mx=-Infinity;
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){ if(ST[i]<mn)mn=ST[i]; if(ST[i]>mx)mx=ST[i]; }
    const nb=40;
    const bins=new Int32Array(nb);
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){
      const b=Math.min(nb-1, Math.floor((ST[i]-mn)/(mx-mn)*nb));
      bins[b]++;
    }
    let maxB=0; for(const v of bins) if(v>maxB) maxB=v;
    const X=s=>xL+(s-mn)/(mx-mn)*(xR-xL);
    const Y=c=>yB-(c/maxB)*(yB-yT);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:yB,x2:xR,y2:yB,stroke:'var(--line)'}));
    for(let b=0;b<nb;b++){
      const sLo=mn+(b/nb)*(mx-mn);
      const sHi=mn+((b+1)/nb)*(mx-mn);
      const x1=X(sLo), x2=X(sHi);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:x1,y:Y(bins[b]),width:Math.max(0,x2-x1-1),height:yB-Y(bins[b]),fill:'var(--violet)',opacity:0.55}));
    }
    // strike line
    if(K>=mn && K<=mx){
      const xk=X(K);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xk,y1:yT,x2:xk,y2:yB,stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-dasharray':'3 4','stroke-width':1.2}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:xk,y:yT-6,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--yellow)'});
      t.textContent='K='+K; svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const s=mn+(i/4)*(mx-mn);
      const xp=X(s);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xp,y1:yB,x2:xp,y2:yB+4,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:xp,y:yB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=s.toFixed(0); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    const xl=SVG('text',{x:(xL+xR)/2,y:H-4,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    xl.textContent='terminal asset price S_T'; svg.appendChild(xl);
    out.textContent =
      `parameters:  S₀=${S0}, K=${K}, r=${r}, σ=${sig.toFixed(2)}, T=${T.toFixed(2)},  N=${N} paths\n`+
      `Monte Carlo price  e^{−rT}·𝔼̂[max(Sₜ−K,0)]  =  ${mc.toFixed(4)}\n`+
      `standard error                              =  ${se.toFixed(4)}\n`+
      `Black–Scholes closed form                   =  ${bs.toFixed(4)}\n`+
      `relative error                              =  ${(Math.abs(mc-bs)/bs*100).toFixed(2)} %\n\n`+
      `Histogram: simulated S_T under 𝐐 (lognormal). The portion of mass right of K=${K} contributes to the call payoff.`;
  }
  NIn.addEventListener('input',()=>{NV.textContent='N = '+NIn.value;});
  $('#mc-run').addEventListener('click', run);
  run();
})();
</script>

4. Optimal portfolio selection (Merton)

Pricing solves "what is this payoff worth?" The complementary question is "how should I invest in the first place?" Merton (1969) framed it as a dynamic optimization. Let $W_t$ denote wealth, and let an investor allocate fraction $\pi_t$ of wealth to the risky asset $S_t$ and the rest to the bond, consuming at rate $c_t\ge 0$. Wealth evolves as $$dW_t \;=\; \bigl[(r + \pi_t(\mu - r))W_t - c_t\bigr]dt \;+\; \pi_t \sigma W_t\,dB_t.$$ The investor seeks to maximize $$\mathbb{E}\!\int_0^T e^{-\rho t}\,u(c_t)\,dt \;+\; e^{-\rho T}\,U(W_T)$$ over admissible feedback controls $(c_t,\pi_t)$, for a utility $u$ — usually constant relative risk aversion: $u(c)=c^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)$, with $\gamma>0$, $\gamma\ne 1$.

The closed form. Because CRRA utility is homogeneous of degree $1-\gamma$, the value function separates: $V(t,w) = \phi(t)\,w^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)$ for some deterministic $\phi$. Plugging into the HJB equation (next section), the optimal portfolio fraction is $$\boxed{\;\pi^* \;=\; \frac{\mu - r}{\gamma\,\sigma^2}\;}$$ — the Merton fraction. It's the Sharpe ratio $(\mu-r)/\sigma$ divided by $\gamma\sigma$, equivalently the excess return divided by risk-aversion-weighted variance. Crucially, $\pi^*$ does not depend on wealth $w$ or on the horizon $T$. Higher Sharpe ratios mean larger positions; higher risk aversion ($\gamma\uparrow$) or higher volatility ($\sigma\uparrow$) shrink the position toward zero (and can flip its sign when $\mu<r$).

5. The Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation

The Merton result generalizes. Let $X_t\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be a controlled diffusion $$dX_t \;=\; b(t,X_t,u_t)\,dt \;+\; \sigma(t,X_t,u_t)\,dB_t,$$ where the control $u_t\in U\subset\mathbb{R}^k$ is chosen by an agent observing $X_t$. Given a running reward $f(t,x,u)$ and a terminal reward $g(x)$, the value function is $$V(t,x) \;=\; \sup_{u}\,\mathbb{E}_{t,x}\!\left[\int_t^T f(s,X_s,u_s)\,ds \;+\; g(X_T)\right].$$ Dynamic programming gives the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation: $$\partial_t V \;+\; \sup_{u\in U}\!\Bigl\{\mathcal{L}^u V(t,x) + f(t,x,u)\Bigr\} \;=\; 0, \qquad V(T,x)=g(x),$$ with $\mathcal{L}^u V = b\cdot\nabla V + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\sigma\sigma^\top \nabla^2 V\bigr)$ the generator of $X$ under control $u$.

The supremum makes HJB nonlinear, in contrast to Feynman–Kac which is linear (the controlled process is fixed, only the expectation is computed). The argmax inside is an optimal feedback control $u^*(t,x)$. A verification theorem establishes that any smooth solution $V$ of the HJB equation satisfying suitable growth/terminal conditions equals the value function and the candidate $u^*$ is optimal — sufficient conditions for what dynamic programming derives heuristically.

Merton revisited. For Merton's problem with CRRA utility and no consumption, take state $X_t=W_t$, control $\pi$, $b = (r+\pi(\mu-r))w$, $\sigma = \pi\sigma w$. Substituting the ansatz $V(t,w)=\phi(t)w^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)$ and computing $\sup_\pi$ analytically reproduces $\pi^*=(\mu-r)/(\gamma\sigma^2)$, with $\phi$ an ODE in $t$. The closed-form Merton result is the canonical example of a solvable HJB.

<script>
/* §5 — discrete-time HJB on a binomial tree */
(function(){
  const svg=$('#hjb-svg'), out=$('#hjb-out');
  const rhoIn=$('#hjb-rho'), rhoV=$('#hjb-rhov');
  const W=760, H=360, xL=60, xR=W-30, yT=40, yB=H-40;
  const N=5; // depth
  // states: at time i, nodes 0..i, i+1 total
  // payoff at terminal: g(i, j) = j - i/2 (signed deviation, optimization is over up/down moves with values v[i][j]; here we just maximize a CRRA-like reward)
  // We'll do a *value-iteration* visualization: at each step, fill backward from leaves.
  let stepIdx=N+1; // start: only leaves shown
  function reset(){ stepIdx=N+1; render(); }
  function step(){ if(stepIdx>0) stepIdx--; render(); }
  function nodeXY(i,j){
    const x=xL + (i/N)*(xR-xL);
    const y=yT + ((j+0.5)/(i+1))*(yB-yT);
    return {x,y};
  }
  // value function: terminal g(j) = sqrt(j+1) (concave utility-like)
  // backward: V(i,j) = max_action ( beta * (V(i+1,j) + V(i+1,j+1))/2 ) — here action is implicit, the max over up/down has been absorbed since they're equivalent in this toy.
  // To make the "max" visible we compute two candidate actions:
  //   action A: take the up move only -> V(i+1,j+1)
  //   action B: take the down move only -> V(i+1,j)
  //   action C: mix 50/50 -> (V(i+1,j)+V(i+1,j+1))/2
  // Then V(i,j) = beta * max(A,B,C).  For monotone g, C is rarely optimal — but we keep all three so the user sees the sup_u operator at work.
  function recompute(){
    const beta=+rhoIn.value;
    const V=[];
    for(let i=0;i<=N;i++){ V.push(new Array(i+1).fill(NaN)); }
    // leaves
    for(let j=0;j<=N;j++) V[N][j]=Math.sqrt(j+1);
    // fill backward only up to stepIdx
    for(let i=N-1;i>=stepIdx;i--){
      for(let j=0;j<=i;j++){
        const a=V[i+1][j+1];
        const b=V[i+1][j];
        const c=0.5*(a+b);
        V[i][j]=beta*Math.max(a,b,c);
      }
    }
    return {V, beta};
  }
  function render(){
    const {V, beta}=recompute();
    rhoV.textContent='β = '+beta.toFixed(3);
    svg.innerHTML='';
    // edges
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){
      for(let j=0;j<=i;j++){
        const p=nodeXY(i,j), pu=nodeXY(i+1,j+1), pd=nodeXY(i+1,j);
        svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:p.x,y1:p.y,x2:pu.x,y2:pu.y,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.8,opacity:0.5}));
        svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:p.x,y1:p.y,x2:pd.x,y2:pd.y,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.8,opacity:0.5}));
      }
    }
    // nodes
    for(let i=0;i<=N;i++){
      for(let j=0;j<=i;j++){
        const p=nodeXY(i,j);
        const v=V[i][j];
        const filled = !isNaN(v);
        const isLeaf = i===N;
        const fill = filled ? (isLeaf?'var(--cyan)':'var(--pink)') : 'var(--panel2)';
        const stroke = filled ? 'var(--ink)' : 'var(--mute)';
        svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:p.x,cy:p.y,r:14,fill,stroke,'stroke-width':1.0,opacity:0.85}));
        if(filled){
          const t=SVG('text',{x:p.x,y:p.y+4,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':10,fill:'var(--ink)','font-weight':600});
          t.textContent=v.toFixed(2); svg.appendChild(t);
        } else {
          const t=SVG('text',{x:p.x,y:p.y+4,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
          t.textContent='?'; svg.appendChild(t);
        }
      }
    }
    // x-axis labels: time
    for(let i=0;i<=N;i++){
      const p=nodeXY(i,0);
      const t=SVG('text',{x:p.x,y:yB+20,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent='t='+i; svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // status
    let status;
    if(stepIdx>N) status='terminal leaves V(N,j)=√(j+1).  click "step Bellman" to fill backward.';
    else if(stepIdx===0) status='fully solved.  the root value V(0,0) is the optimal expected utility.';
    else status='filled rows '+stepIdx+'..'+N+'.  next step computes V('+(stepIdx-1)+',·) = β · max( upper, lower, mix ).';
    const root = V[0][0];
    const display = isNaN(root) ? '— (compute backward to reach root)' : root.toFixed(3);
    out.textContent =
      'binomial tree, depth N='+N+', discount β='+beta.toFixed(3)+'\n'+
      'terminal utility g(j) = √(j+1)   (concave, mimics CRRA)\n\n'+
      'Bellman recursion:\n'+
      '   V(i,j) = β · sup_u 𝔼[ V(i+1, j+a(u)) ]   with three candidate actions u: always-up, always-down, mix.\n\n'+
      status+'\n\nroot value V(0,0) = '+display;
  }
  rhoIn.addEventListener('input', render);
  $('#hjb-step').addEventListener('click', step);
  $('#hjb-reset').addEventListener('click', reset);
  render();
})();
</script>

6. Itô diffusions in finance

Three Itô-calculus facts do most of the work in derivatives pricing:

  • Quadratic variation. For an Itô process $dX_t = b\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, $d\langle X\rangle_t = \sigma^2\,dt$. Hedging error variance is a quadratic-variation integral of the mis-hedged piece.
  • Itô's formula. $df(X_t) = f'(X_t)\,dX_t + \tfrac{1}{2}f''(X_t)\,d\langle X\rangle_t$. The second term is the source of the $\partial_{SS}$ in the Black–Scholes PDE.
  • Itô isometry. $\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bigl(\int_0^T\theta_t\,dB_t\bigr)^2\bigr] = \mathbb{E}\int_0^T\theta_t^2\,dt$. Quantifies hedging-error variance as a single $L^2$ integral.

blocks.html: Self-financing portfolios. A portfolio holding $\Delta_t$ shares and $\beta_t$ in the riskless bond, with total wealth $W_t=\Delta_t S_t+\beta_t e^{rt}$, is self-financing if no external cash is added or removed: $dW_t = \Delta_t\,dS_t + r\beta_t e^{rt}\,dt$. The hedging derivation builds a self-financing portfolio that replicates the option payoff at maturity — and by no-arbitrage, its current cost must equal the option price.

7. Beyond Black–Scholes

The Black–Scholes formula is calibrated to one parameter per option: implied volatility $\sigma_{\mathrm{imp}}$, the $\sigma$ that makes the formula return the observed price. If Black–Scholes were correct, $\sigma_{\mathrm{imp}}(K,T)$ would be flat in $K$. Empirically, it isn't: in equity options the implied surface shows a volatility smile (U-shaped in $K$ for short maturities) and a skew (lower strikes carry higher vol — out-of-the-money puts price in crash risk). This is the "working empirical object" that any post-Black–Scholes model must fit.

Three families of extensions dominate practice:

  • Stochastic volatility (Heston 1993). Volatility itself follows an SDE: $$dS_t = \mu S_t\,dt + \sqrt{v_t}\,S_t\,dB_t^{(1)}, \qquad dv_t = \kappa(\theta-v_t)\,dt+\xi\sqrt{v_t}\,dB_t^{(2)},$$ with $B^{(1)},B^{(2)}$ correlated. Two Brownian drivers, one tradable: the market is incomplete and the volatility-risk premium is a free parameter calibrated to market prices.
  • Jump-diffusion (Merton 1976). Add a compound Poisson process: $dS_t/S_{t-} = \mu\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t + (J-1)\,dN_t$, where $N$ is Poisson with rate $\lambda$ and $J$ is the random jump multiplier. Captures fat tails and crash risk in a tractable way — the resulting PDE has an integral term but pricing remains closed-form for European options.
  • Local volatility (Dupire 1994). Take $\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}(t,S)$ as a deterministic function of state, chosen to exactly fit the entire implied surface via the Dupire formula $$\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}^2(K,T) \;=\; \frac{2\,\partial_T C(K,T)}{K^2\,\partial_{KK}C(K,T)}.$$ No new randomness, but the surface determines the local dynamics — and the model is famously bad at predicting how the surface itself evolves.

<script>
/* §7 — implied vol surface shapes */
(function(){
  const svg=$('#vs-svg'), out=$('#vs-out');
  const bFlat=$('#vs-flat'), bSmile=$('#vs-smile'), bSkew=$('#vs-skew');
  const W=760, H=320, xL=60, xR=W-30, yT=30, yB=H-40;
  let mode='flat';
  function impVol(m, mode){
    // m = log-moneyness log(K/F)
    if(mode==='flat') return 0.22;
    if(mode==='smile') return 0.22 + 0.18*m*m;
    if(mode==='skew')  return 0.22 - 0.30*m + 0.16*m*m;
    return 0.22;
  }
  function draw(){
    svg.innerHTML='';
    bFlat.classList.toggle('active', mode==='flat');
    bSmile.classList.toggle('active', mode==='smile');
    bSkew.classList.toggle('active', mode==='skew');
    const mMin=-0.5, mMax=0.5;
    let vMax=0.0;
    for(let i=0;i<=200;i++){
      const m=mMin+(i/200)*(mMax-mMin);
      const v=impVol(m,mode);
      if(v>vMax) vMax=v;
    }
    const vMin=0.05, vMaxA=Math.max(vMax,0.5)*1.1;
    const X=m=>xL+(m-mMin)/(mMax-mMin)*(xR-xL);
    const Y=v=>yB-(v-vMin)/(vMaxA-vMin)*(yB-yT);
    // axes
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:yB,x2:xR,y2:yB,stroke:'var(--line)'}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:yT,x2:xL,y2:yB,stroke:'var(--line)'}));
    // moneyness = 1 line
    const xAtm=X(0);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xAtm,y1:yT,x2:xAtm,y2:yB,stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-dasharray':'3 4'}));
    const t=SVG('text',{x:xAtm,y:yT-6,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--yellow)'});
    t.textContent='ATM (K=F)'; svg.appendChild(t);
    // implied-vol curve
    let d='';
    for(let i=0;i<=200;i++){
      const m=mMin+(i/200)*(mMax-mMin);
      const v=impVol(m,mode);
      d += (i===0?'M':'L')+X(m)+','+Y(v)+' ';
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d,fill:'none',stroke:'var(--pink)','stroke-width':2}));
    // x ticks
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const m=mMin+(i/4)*(mMax-mMin);
      const xp=X(m);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xp,y1:yB,x2:xp,y2:yB+4,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:xp,y:yB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=m.toFixed(2); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // y ticks
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const v=vMin+(i/4)*(vMaxA-vMin);
      const yp=Y(v);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL-4,y1:yp,x2:xL,y2:yp,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:xL-8,y:yp+4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=v.toFixed(2); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    const xl=SVG('text',{x:(xL+xR)/2,y:H-4,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    xl.textContent='log-moneyness  log(K/F)'; svg.appendChild(xl);
    const yl=SVG('text',{x:14,y:yT+(yB-yT)/2,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)',transform:`rotate(-90 14 ${yT+(yB-yT)/2})`});
    yl.textContent='implied volatility σ_imp'; svg.appendChild(yl);
    // readout
    const sigATM=impVol(0,mode);
    const sigUp=impVol(0.2,mode);
    const sigDn=impVol(-0.2,mode);
    const labels={flat:'flat (Black–Scholes)', smile:'symmetric smile (Heston-ish)', skew:'skew (equity-index style)'};
    out.textContent =
      'mode:  '+labels[mode]+'\n\n'+
      'sample implied vols:\n'+
      `   K/F = e^{−0.2} (OTM put):   σ_imp = ${sigDn.toFixed(3)}\n`+
      `   K = F   (ATM):              σ_imp = ${sigATM.toFixed(3)}\n`+
      `   K/F = e^{+0.2} (OTM call):  σ_imp = ${sigUp.toFixed(3)}\n\n`+
      (mode==='flat' ? 'flat surface = Black–Scholes is the true generator.  empirically false.' :
       mode==='smile' ? 'smile = symmetric heavy tails.  produced by stochastic-vol models (Heston).' :
       'skew = OTM puts overpriced relative to BS.  reflects crash-risk premium in equity markets.');
  }
  bFlat.addEventListener('click',()=>{ mode='flat'; draw(); });
  bSmile.addEventListener('click',()=>{ mode='smile'; draw(); });
  bSkew.addEventListener('click',()=>{ mode='skew'; draw(); });
  draw();
})();
</script>

8. Connections

Mathematical finance is the most operational application of stochastic calculus: every line of the derivation has a counterpart on a trader's screen, and conversely every market irregularity tells you something about the modelling assumption that broke. The flow of ideas outward:

  • Stochastic calculus — Itô's formula — the technical engine for delta-hedging and PDE derivation; without $(dB)^2 = dt$ no Black–Scholes correction term appears.
  • Stochastic calculus — Girsanov's theorem — the change-of-measure that turns the historical asset into a discounted martingale, i.e. the foundation of risk-neutral pricing.
  • Partial differential equations — the heat equation — Black–Scholes is the heat equation in log-price coordinates; numerical PDE solvers (finite difference, finite element) are an industrial-strength alternative to Monte Carlo.
  • Stochastic processes and martingales — the martingale framework provides the language (filtrations, stopping times, optional sampling) in which American-option pricing, fundamental theorems of asset pricing, and martingale-representation-driven hedging are all stated.
  • Dynamical systems — verification theorems for HJB connect optimal-control PDEs to viscosity solutions, the standard framework when value functions are merely continuous; the same framework appears in front-propagation, image processing, and reinforcement learning.

Open frontiers: rough-volatility models (Bayer–Friz–Gatheral, fractional Brownian drivers with $H<1/2$ — empirically a better fit to the term-structure of implied vol than Heston); machine-learning calibration of model-free option pricing; market-microstructure-aware optimal execution (Almgren–Chriss, Cartea–Jaimungal); equilibrium models that endogenize $\mu$ rather than treating it as a model input.
